items.name: Sleeping bag for a home without heat
items.need: If heat fails in winter, a warm sleeping bag lets each person stay warm in bed without burning anything indoors.
items.how_to_choose: Go by the comfort rating, not the number in the name: a bag sold as a '20' is often comfortable only to the low or mid 30s F. Look for a comfort rating of 32 F (0 C) or lower, or plan a blanket over the bag, and add a wool hat and a layer under you. Synthetic fill costs less, keeps some warmth if it gets damp and is easier to wash; down is lighter and packs far smaller for the same warmth, costs more and must be kept dry. A rectangular cut is roomier and can open out as a quilt on the sofa; a mummy cut is warmer for its weight and tighter. The warmest bags here weigh 8 to 12 lb and roll up as big as a duffel bag; the Compact pick weighs under 3 lb and packs to about 8 x 13 in.

qty.note: One bag for each adult and child. Not for a baby: a baby sleeps on a firm, flat surface of their own, never in a sleeping bag.

items.already_own: A good comforter plus a wool blanket on top, or any sleeping bag in the household, is enough for a mild cold snap. Test by sleeping in it in a cold room before you need it.

safety_notes.text: Hypothermia warning signs in adults are shivering, exhaustion, confusion, fumbling hands, memory loss, slurred speech and drowsiness. In infants, look for bright red, cold skin and very low energy. A body temperature below 95 F is a medical emergency: get help, and warm the person while you wait.
safety_notes.source_title: Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm

safety_notes.text: To stay warm indoors without heat: use extra blankets, close off unused rooms, block drafts at the bottom of doors, and close curtains at night. Check on older adults often because they may make less body heat.
safety_notes.source_title: Safety Guidelines: During & After a Winter Storm

safety_notes.text: Fuel-burning heating can produce carbon monoxide, an odorless and deadly gas. Put CO alarms on every level and outside sleeping areas and test them monthly. Use portable generators outdoors only, at least 20 feet from the home. Keep electric space heaters 3 feet from anything that burns, plug them straight into a wall outlet and turn them off when you sleep.
safety_notes.source_title: Keep Warm and Safe This Winter: Tips for Using Generators, Furnaces and Space Heaters (Jan 23, 2026)

safety_notes.text: A sleeping bag is not for a baby. CDC says to put a baby to sleep on their back on a firm, flat surface, in a sleep area of their own such as a crib or bassinet in the room where you sleep, with soft bedding such as blankets and pillows kept out and the baby's head left uncovered.
safety_notes.source_title: Providing Care for Babies to Sleep Safely

items.name: Window insulation film kit (and draft stopper)
items.need: Single-pane and leaky windows lose a lot of heat; clear shrink film and a door draft stopper hold warmth in a room you heat with body heat or a safe electric heater.
items.how_to_choose: Pick a kit by window count and size, and check the tape is rated for your frame. Duck Brand says its tape is safe for renters on painted wood, aluminum and vinyl but not on plaster, drywall or unfinished wood. Film goes on the inside and shrinks tight with a hair dryer. For under doors, a long fabric tube filled with rice or sand, or a rolled towel, works as a renter-safe draft stopper; this page picks no draft-stopper product.

qty.note: One kit covers about 3-5 standard windows; add a second kit if you have more windows.

items.already_own: Clear plastic sheeting plus painter's tape works in a pinch, and a rolled towel works as a draft stopper. A heavy lined curtain closed at night also helps.

safety_notes.text: To stay warm indoors without heat: use extra blankets, close off unused rooms, block drafts at the bottom of doors, and close curtains at night. Check on older adults often because they may make less body heat.

items.name: Battery fan
items.need: A fan that runs from a battery or a power bank, not the grid, keeps air moving in a stuffy home during a summer outage.
items.how_to_choose: Two things matter: how far the breeze reaches and how long the fan runs. Pocket and desk fans reach 2 to 4 ft, enough for one person; a larger fan reaches 10 ft or more and can cool a room of people, but in Outdoor Life's test the large fans ran only 2 to 5.5 hours on high. Outdoor Life measured runtime on high speed only; a low speed lasts longer, but no test of it was found. Check what powers the fan, because that sets the cost of keeping it running for days: built-in cells charged by USB-C, AA cells, a tool-battery pack that needs its own charger, or a separate power bank. In the same test one $15 clip-on fan would not hold a charge, so pick a model with a test behind it.

qty.note: One per household; more if people sleep in separate rooms.

items.already_own: Any USB desk fan works from a power bank. A 10,000 mAh bank (about 37 Wh) runs a 5 W fan for roughly 6-7 hours; check the fan's watt rating.

safety_notes.text: Fuel-burning heating can produce carbon monoxide, an odorless and deadly gas. Put CO alarms on every level and outside sleeping areas and test them monthly. Use portable generators outdoors only, at least 20 feet from the home. Keep electric space heaters 3 feet from anything that burns, plug them straight into a wall outlet and turn them off when you sleep.
safety_notes.source_title: Keep Warm and Safe This Winter: Tips for Using Generators, Furnaces and Space Heaters (Jan 23, 2026)

items.name: Cooler
items.need: When the fridge warms in an outage, a cooler packed with ice keeps perishables at or below 40 F so you do not have to throw everything out.
items.how_to_choose: What matters is how long the cooler keeps food at or below 40 F, and how much it holds. A 50 to 60 quart cooler takes the perishables from a household fridge plus the ice to keep them cold; it is 26 to 30 in long, weighs 15 to 31 lb empty and far more when full. Pre-chill it, fill it mostly with ice, and keep it closed. Test results vary a lot between publications because test conditions differ, so compare within one test. A cooler of about 20 quarts is far easier to carry and store; it holds a day or two of food for one or two people, or refrigerated medicines (X7-02) with a few frozen packs.
items.already_own: Any hard cooler with a tight lid works. Put a fridge thermometer inside it: food in a cooler follows the same rule as food in the fridge.

safety_notes.text: With no thermometer, treat fridge food as unsafe once the power has been off for 4 hours with the door kept shut. With a thermometer in the fridge, throw out meat, poultry, fish, eggs, milk and leftovers once they have been above 40 °F for more than 2 hours. Frozen food that still has ice crystals, or is at 40 °F or colder, can be refrozen or cooked. Never taste food to test it.

items.name: Low-wattage electric kettle
items.need: Hot water is an extra, not part of the plan: every meal in this plan can be eaten cold. If you own a power station that can run one, a small electric kettle heats water for drinks or instant meals with no flame indoors.
items.how_to_choose: Check the watts first: most power stations under 300 W of inverter output cannot run a kettle at all. Heating one quart takes roughly 95 to 115 Wh whatever the kettle's wattage, so a 300 Wh station gives only about two to three quarts, and a 300 W kettle needs at least 20 minutes per quart. items.name: Manual evacuation stair chair
items.need: If someone at home cannot walk down stairs and the elevators stop, an evacuation chair lets trained helpers take them down a stairwell.
items.how_to_choose: Ask your building manager first: many high-rises already hold evacuation chairs and have a plan. Treat any chair as a candidate until you have read the current manual for the exact model. Check the maximum working load in the manual, not in the advert, against the person plus clothing and equipment, and ask the maker which test the figure comes from: the RESNA standard for these chairs, ED-1, was still a draft when checked. Have the supplier train the helpers on your own stairs.

qty.note: One per household that needs it; check with building management before buying.

items.already_own: Many buildings, especially high-rises and schools, already keep stair chairs and have staff trained to use them. Ask management and ask to be added to the evacuation list before you buy.

safety_notes.text: ED-1, the RESNA standard for emergency stair travel devices, sets performance and test rules (weight capacity, stability, dynamic load, maneuverability) and requires makers to publish dimensions and occupant weight capacity. The weight-capacity test uses a manikin equal to a 99th-percentile adult male, about 350 lb; heavier loads need added weight. Inspection is required at least every 12 months and after each evacuation or drill. The standard was out for public comment in 2025.
RESNA ED-1 is the standard for emergency stair travel devices used by individuals with disabilities; the RESNA page describes it as a final draft and gives no year.

item_flags: One candidate, not a pick: the Evacusafe Excel tracked evacuation chair, $1,795 at the maker's US store and 30 lb. The maker's product page and data sheet say it carries 500 lb, but the operating manual linked from the same page gives a maximum working load of 400 lb, and none names a test standard. Plan on the lower figure and ask the maker in writing which applies.

Before buying any chair, get the current manual for the exact model and have building management, the supplier and the person's occupational therapist or mobility specialist check the fit, the rated load, your stairs and landings, storage, upkeep and how many trained helpers it needs. Write down another way out, and the point at which the person leaves early, in case any of this cannot be met.
A chair alone does not make a stairwell safe: it needs trained helpers and practice, and a stairwell may be full of other people or smoke. This is this site's judgement, not an official source's.

items.name: Two-way radios
items.need: When phones and internet fail, handheld radios let family and neighbors talk within a building or a block.
items.how_to_choose: The minimum is two radios: one for each group that will be apart. Buy the same model for everyone so they share channels. There are four kinds, and what the FCC asks differs. FRS: no license, 22 channels, at most 2 watts. GMRS: the same channels with more power, plus mobile radios and repeaters; it needs a license, which you can apply for at 18, which lasts 10 years and which covers your family members of any age. CB: no license, 40 channels on a different band, so a CB set does not talk to FRS or GMRS radios. Ham (amateur) radio has the most bands and the longest reach, but each person who transmits needs their own license, earned by passing a written exam given by volunteer examiners; most people start with the Technician class. The picks here are FRS and GMRS hand-helds, because those are the kinds testers have compared; no tester's pick for a CB or ham set was found. Claimed ranges of 25-35 miles are for open line of sight; in a city expect far less. No test of range inside concrete buildings was found: Outdoor Life measured about 0.3-0.6 mi with trees and hills in the way, and a concrete high-rise will cut that much further. Plan on a few floors or one building, not blocks, and test them before you need them.

qty.note: Two radios is the minimum: one for each group that will be apart. A two-pack counts as two; a radio sold singly is bought twice. Add one radio for each extra group.

items.already_own: Any FRS radios you own work with FRS-only radios on the same channel. Many cheap 22-channel radios are FRS/GMRS hybrids; use them only on FRS channels at FRS power unless you hold a GMRS license.

safety_notes.text: FRS radios need no individual license, and anyone of any age may use one. GMRS needs an FCC license: you must be 18 to apply, and with a license any family member, of any age, can use the radios. FRS power is 2 W on channels 1 to 7 and 15 to 22 and 0.5 W on channels 8 to 14; the FCC says the usual range on the half-watt channels is under half a mile. CB needs no individual license. Amateur (ham) radio needs a license for each operator, earned by examination.
safety_notes.source_title: Family Radio Service (FRS); General Mobile Radio Service (GMRS); Citizens Band Radio Service; Amateur Radio Service
